content.text: Fracture of the wrist and hand is very common. Common types include distal radius, scaphoid, and hand (metacarpal) fractures.

items: Most common distal radius fracture
Dorsal displacement of distal fracture segment
"Dinner fork" appearance
MOI: FOOSH on an extended wrist
Distal radius fracture
Volar displacement of distal fracture segment
"Dinner spoon" appearance
MOI: FOOSH on a flexed wrist
MOI: FOOSH, particularly on extended and pronated wrist
Susceptible to avascular necrosis following fracture
If avascular necrosis occurs, SLAC wrist (a type of arthritis) may develop — can lead to instability and be very debilitating
MOI: falls, crush injury, tendon avulsion, direct trauma
Swelling may or may not occur
Generalised hesitation to active motion is a strong sign of hand fracture
ORIF (surgery): area immobilised in orthosis/brace, but early movement can begin shortly after
Non-surgical: cast/immobilisation, typically 4-6 weeks before any movement allowed
Edema
Limited ROM
Limited joint mobility
Muscle weakness
Secondary problems in shoulder and elbow function
Have you had consolidation (full radiographic healing) confirmed by MD?
Has your doctor cleared you to receive massage?
Did you have surgery?
Is there any internal fixation (rods, screws, pins, plates)?
Is there a surgical scar? How does the scar feel?
Were you immobilised? In what position? For how long? What type? When was it removed?
Do you know of any other tissue injury (muscle, ligament, blood vessel, or nerve)?
Have you noticed any changes to sensation in the area?
How is the tissue quality? Does the skin feel healthy? Have you noticed any muscle atrophy?
Have you received any other treatment? Can you describe it and whether it has helped?
AROM is usually reduced in all ranges, with greatest reductions in wrist ROM and supination
PROM is similar to AROM
RROM is reduced in all ranges
May be performed following consolidation
Can be used to develop a baseline for all muscles of the forearm and hand
Joint play assessment may be performed following consolidation
Often shows capsular restrictions at the wrist
Grip strength and different types of grip (precision, power) are generally reduced

content.text: Treat as per general fracture treatment. If surgery was performed, learn about and follow any post-surgical instructions.

items: Improve muscle and joint health
Restore neuromuscular control and resting muscle tone of area
Reduce contractures or adhesions and promote functional scar tissue
Treat compensatory structures to restore overall function
Decrease adhesions and promote functional scar tissue on surgical scar using skin rolling and frictions
Promote joint health and normal joint play using PROM of wrist, hand, elbow, shoulder
Normalise muscle tone with origin-insertion techniques
Promote neuromuscular control using gentle muscle setting exercises
Improve overall upper limb function with petrissage, NMT, and MFR to scapula, shoulder, upper arm, forearm, and hand

content.title: Cautions — Pre-consolidation or Unknown Consolidation
content.text: Do not traction the affected bone. Do not perform POP in either assessment or treatment. Do not use deep, aggressive techniques. Do not perform joint mobilisation or stretching.

content.title: Cautions — With Internal Fixation
content.text: Modify hydrotherapy to avoid prolonged applications of extreme temperatures.

content.title: Cautions — Poor Tissue Health / Atrophy
content.text: Avoid deep longitudinal strokes or aggressive manipulation of tissue. Avoid MFR if skin health is poor. Do not stretch atrophied muscle.
Restoration of full ROM may take 4-6 weeks. Restoration of strength (grip strength, intrinsic hand muscles) takes longer and may require up to 12 weeks.

Should include: stage (before or after consolidation), severity (how limited is function), and summary of overall impairments. Example: 'Patient presentation is consistent with the effects of post-immobilisation disuse to moderate severity. Full consolidation confirmed.'

quiz.question: A Colle's fracture involves dorsal displacement and results from a FOOSH on which type of wrist position?
quiz.explanation: A Colle's fracture includes dorsal displacement of the distal fracture segment and typically occurs from a FOOSH on an extended wrist ("dinner fork" appearance).

quiz.question: Why is scaphoid fracture of particular concern?
options: It is susceptible to avascular necrosis
It always involves the radius as well
quiz.explanation: The scaphoid is susceptible to avascular necrosis following fracture, which can lead to SLAC wrist (a type of arthritis) and be very debilitating.

quiz.question: It is safe to perform joint mobilisation and stretching before consolidation has been confirmed.
quiz.explanation: Pre-consolidation: Do not perform joint mobilisation or stretching. Do not traction the affected bone. Do not do POP in assessment or treatment. Do not use deep, aggressive techniques.
